lines.text: An island of ancient Buddhist kingdoms, spice coasts and tea hills, of war and of recovery. This is the long story of Sri Lanka.
The first great kingdom of the island grew at Anuradhapura, and in the third century BCE Buddhism arrived there, to shape the island ever after.
Around 160 BCE King Dutugamunu united the island under one rule, and the old chronicles made him a hero.
Centuries later King Kashyapa built his fortress on top of a great rock at Sigiriya, its walls painted with graceful maidens.
In the eleventh century power moved to Polonnaruwa, a medieval capital whose ruins still stand among the trees.
In the hills, Kandy rose, and it would become the capital of the last Sinhala kingdom.
From the sea came Europeans. At Galle on the south coast, first the Portuguese and then the Dutch built a mighty fort.
In Kandy, the Temple of the Tooth guarded the island's most sacred relic, a tooth of the Buddha.
In 1815 the British took Kandy, and with it the whole island. Ceylon was a British colony for over a century.
In 1867 tea was planted on a large scale in the hills, and Ceylon tea became known around the world.
S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike would become prime minister, make Sinhala the only official language, and be assassinated in 1959.
His widow Sirimavo took his place, and in 1960 became the world's first woman prime minister.
Mahinda Rajapaksa, as president, would one day end a long civil war.
In 1948 Ceylon became independent from Britain. In 1972 it took a new name, Sri Lanka.
His brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa would later become president, and flee the country in the protests of 2022.
Anura Kumara Dissanayake would become president in 2024, after the crisis.
On the cricket field, Sanath Jayasuriya changed the game with his fearless fast scoring.
And Muttiah Muralitharan, the spin bowler, would take more Test wickets than anyone in history.
In 1982 Sri Lanka began playing Test cricket, and soon the team was among the world's best.
In 1983 civil war broke out between the government and the Tamil Tigers. It would last for twenty-six years.
In 1996, amid the war, the nation found joy: Sri Lanka won the Cricket World Cup.
On Boxing Day 2004 a huge earthquake off Sumatra sent giant waves across the ocean, and Sri Lanka's coasts were among the worst hit.
Ten years after the war ended, on Easter Sunday 2019, suicide bombers struck churches and hotels, killing two hundred and sixty-nine people.
That same year an economic crisis began, and by 2022 the country could not pay its debts.
Then the people rose. In 2022 huge protests filled the streets, and the president fled.
From Anuradhapura's shrines to the protests of today, Sri Lanka's story keeps finding new beginnings.
